Native YouTube App Lands on CarPlay With Open-Source Project
14 photos
Photo: GitHub
People have been asking for a way to watch YouTube on Android Auto and CarPlay for quite some time, and while third-party methods have existed for a while, an official YouTube app for cars is still nowhere to be seen.
That’s changing today with the release of YouDash, also referred to as YouTube Car, an open-source project whose purpose is to enable the native YouTube app on CarPlay.
Documented on GitHub , this application allows users to watch their favorite videos directly on their infotainment screens. Obviously, you’re only supposed to do this while the vehicle is parked for safety reasons, but the application will also work while you’re in motion. So before reading the rest of the article, just remember that this application must be used only while you’re stationary because otherwise, it would become a major distraction source in a second.
This app doesn’t come with any ads and promises a responsive feed, an on-screen keyboard, and a split-screen interface that allows the video to play on the left and see the playlist on the right. YouTube users would certainly find this implementation familiar, as this is the same configuration available on YouTube in the browser.
One of the best things about YouDash is that it can run on pretty much any CarPlay screen, so it doesn’t matter how small or large the infotainment unit is because the application adapts to its dimensions, resolution, and form factor. However, the developer explains that not all these settings have been tested.
Photo: GitHub Worth knowing is that the app won’t run on CarPlay with an iPhone updated to the latest version of iOS. While it’ll work properly on iOS 27.0.1, it won’t do it on iOS 27.3. As I reported not long ago, some video apps that enabled YouTube on CarPlay - not necessarily using the native app but by relying on other methods - also stopped working after the release of the most recent iOS update .
As a result, you’ll need an older version of iOS if you want to run this app in your car.
As for the installation method, it’s not necessarily the most intuitive approach. The app is not available through the App Store - and there’s a good chance it’ll never be - and there is no IPA file to install it manually. You’ll need a developer account and a Mac to install it on your iPhone, at least for the moment, though the developer should certainly find a more straightforward way to do the whole thing.
The step-by-step installation guide is available on GitHub.
Photo: Apple via MacRumors YouTube on Android Auto and CarPlay While YouTube is not yet available on Android Auto and CarPlay, both Google and Apple have paved the way for enabling video apps on their phone projection systems.
Apple enabled video app support on CarPlay with the release of iOS 26.4, suggesting that video apps like YouTube would eventually be fully supported on the platform. This still doesn’t happen, with video apps allowing users to watch videos on CarPlay not allowed on the App Store. Methods to gain the same functionality are still available, though, and they continue to work even after the most recent iOS updates.
Meanwhile, Google is much closer to unlocking YouTube on Android Auto. The company promised this functionality in the spring of this year when it announced that new app categories would be unlocked on Android Auto, including video and browsers. YouTube was supposed to spearhead this new expansion, with the first users originally projected to get the update by the end of 2026.
Most recently, Google said that video apps would land on Android Auto soon , though no further specifics were provided. Similarly, methods to enable YouTube on Android Auto are still available, though without official support. Google has rarely blocked them.
Photo: Apple via MacRumors Once YouTube lands on Android Auto , users will be allowed to watch video apps on their infotainment screens as long as their vehicles are stationary. The video playback will end when the car starts moving, with the experience switching to an audio-only mode where you’re only allowed to listen to the audio track of a video.
This functionality will be offered only if the video apps support it. YouTube will require a Premium subscription to allow the audio mode.
Google hasn’t shared any ETA specifics, but the first beta users are expected to receive the video app support by the end of the year. If everything works properly and no major bugs block the production rollout, the first devices should start getting support for the YouTube app through Google Play Store updates in the first quarter of the next year.
Apple has so far remained tight-lipped on such details, but considering CarPlay updates are still tied to iOS releases, it could take a while until this feature goes live officially. If anything, it’s safe to assume that iOS 28 will include more features on this front.
